sql.payment_reconciliation:
{{ config(materialized='incremental',unique_key='order_id',incremental_strategy='delete+insert') }}
with cash as (select order_id,
 sum(case when kind='capture' and status='succeeded' then amount else 0 end)::bigint as captured,
 sum(case when kind='refund' and status='succeeded' then amount else 0 end)::bigint as returned,
 count(*) filter(where status='failed')::bigint as failed_attempts
 from {{ source('raw','payments') }} group by order_id)
select o.order_id,o.channel,(o.gross-o.discount)::bigint as charged,o.refunded as refund_granted,
 coalesce(captured,0)::bigint as captured,coalesce(returned,0)::bigint as returned,
 (o.gross-o.discount-coalesce(captured,0))::bigint as collection_gap,
 (o.refunded-coalesce(returned,0))::bigint as refund_payable,
 (coalesce(captured,0)-coalesce(returned,0))::bigint as cash_net,
 coalesce(failed_attempts,0)::bigint as failed_attempts
from {{ ref('order_economics') }} o left join cash using(order_id)
{% if is_incremental() %}where o.order_id in ({{ changed_orders() }}){% endif %}
sql.retention:
-- 30-day repurchase, exclusive first date and inclusive day 30; immature users excluded.
with first_order as (
 select customer_id,min(ordered_at) as acquired from {{ source('raw','orders') }} group by customer_id
), customers as (
 select f.customer_id,f.acquired,
 max(case when o.ordered_at>acquired and o.ordered_at<=acquired+30 then 1 else 0 end) as repeated
 from first_order f join {{ source('raw','orders') }} o using(customer_id)
 where acquired<=date '{{ var("as_of", "2026-06-30") }}'-30
 and o.ordered_at<=date '{{ var("as_of", "2026-06-30") }}'
 group by all
)
select date_trunc('month',acquired)::date as cohort,count(*) as eligible_customers,
 sum(repeated)::bigint as repeat_customers, sum(repeated)*1.0/count(*) as retention_30d
from customers group by all

memo.title: 1. Audit discount policy before chasing more volume
memo.evidence: January-to-June discounts increased by ₹369,062.05. Contribution changed by ₹-104,836.06. Review promotion eligibility and contribution per order.
memo.limitation: An accounting decomposition cannot establish that discounts caused the change. Product mix and order volume also changed.

memo.title: 2. Investigate Denim refund reasons
memo.evidence: Denim has the highest store-wide refund-value rate: 4.54% (₹137,920.39 / ₹3,036,355.20 charged); 112/1128 orders received a refund. Check return reasons and product expectations.
memo.limitation: Order-date view includes all loaded refunds. No reason codes or recovered inventory costs exist; recent orders are less mature. This does not prove a quality problem.

memo.title: 3. Review acquisition cohorts before changing ad budgets
memo.evidence: Paid social spent ₹507,900.00 across 258 first-observed customers: CAC ₹1,968.60. Blended net revenue/spend is 4.14× and includes repeat purchases.
memo.limitation: First order in the observed period is not proven lifetime acquisition. Attribution is recorded channel; no causal lift or lifetime-value estimate is available.

replay.kind: Actual DuckDB + dbt executions recorded at build time; browser is read-only

story.title: 1 January · The customer pays ₹120
story.happened: One customer buys two tees at ₹50 each and one cap at ₹30. A ₹10 discount brings the bill to ₹120. They pay ₹70 and ₹50 in two separate payments.
story.testing: Do several products and two payments still count as ONE ₹120 sale?
story.calculation: ₹130 items − ₹10 discount = ₹120 sales. ₹120 − ₹40 item cost − ₹5 delivery cost − ₹2.40 payment fees = ₹72.60 contribution.
story.reason: Add the products once and add the payments separately. Matching every product row to every payment row must not multiply the sale or its costs.
story.action: Both payments add up to the bill. No collection or refund follow-up is needed in this example.

story.title: 4 February · You approve a ₹20 refund
story.happened: The customer receives a ₹20 partial refund approval against the tees bought in January. No money has been returned yet.
story.testing: Does the refund reduce the amount earned once, while showing that ₹20 still needs to be returned?
story.calculation: ₹120 sales − ₹20 approved refund = ₹100 net sales. ₹72.60 previous contribution − ₹20 = ₹52.60. ₹20 approved − ₹0 returned = ₹20 still to return.
story.reason: This project reduces sales when a refund is approved. February records the ₹20 reduction; January stays at ₹72.60 contribution. Across both months the total is ₹52.60. The original item, delivery and payment costs remain expenses.
story.action: Check whether the provider has processed the approved refund. An outstanding amount is a follow-up item, not proof of a failed payment.

story.title: Import again · The same ₹20 refund appears twice
story.happened: The exact same refund record is imported again, with the same refund ID and values. This is not another refund to the customer.
story.testing: Can an export be imported twice without counting the refund twice?
story.calculation: No new refund record is accepted. Net sales stay ₹100; contribution stays ₹52.60; the amount still to return stays ₹20.
story.reason: The existing refund ID identifies an event already counted. A second genuine refund would need a different ID. Changing the values under an existing ID would be rejected.
story.action: No merchant correction is needed for this exact duplicate. The importer reports zero new records.

story.title: 5 February · The provider returns ₹20
story.happened: A successful payment-provider record confirms that ₹20 was returned to the customer. There is no extra refund fee in this synthetic example.
story.testing: Does returning the money clear the outstanding refund WITHOUT reducing sales a second time?
story.calculation: ₹20 approved − ₹20 returned = ₹0 still to return. ₹120 received − ₹20 returned = ₹100 net customer payments. Contribution stays ₹52.60.
story.reason: The reduction in sales was already recorded at approval. This event records the money moving. Deducting another ₹20 from contribution would count one refund twice. Net customer payments are not your bank balance: fees, payouts and other expenses are separate.
story.action: The approved refund now matches a successful return record. This example no longer needs refund-payment follow-up; it does not verify a bank settlement.

story.title: 5 February · A separate ₹10 advertising cost arrives
story.happened: You import ₹10 of advertising cost for this example’s channel. This is a separate business expense, not part of the customer refund.
story.testing: Does an extra cost reduce contribution without changing sales or the customer’s payment balance?
story.calculation: ₹52.60 previous contribution − ₹10 advertising = ₹42.60. Net sales remain ₹100; payments received remain ₹120; returned money remains ₹20.
story.reason: Contribution subtracts the included operating costs from net sales. The cost is recorded at channel level; the tool does not claim that this ad caused the sale or allocate it to a product.
story.action: Include the expense when reviewing channel performance. This example alone cannot tell you whether to cut the campaign.

story.title: 6 February · A ₹1 refund refers to an unknown item
story.happened: An incoming refund record points to an item that is not in the imported orders. The example deliberately supplies this invalid record.
story.testing: Will an unmatched refund be stopped instead of silently changing the report?
story.calculation: The whole incoming batch is rejected. ₹0 is added to refunds. Net sales stay ₹100 and contribution stays ₹42.60. One rejected batch is saved for review.
story.reason: Without an original item, the tool cannot validate the refund. The rejected input is kept separately for investigation (called quarantine in the technical details). It has no effect on the accepted financial totals.
story.action: Find the missing order/item or fix the source mapping, then resubmit. A rejection does not prove fraud and does not establish that the refund is invalid in the real store.
